root.note: Reconstructed by the TLFi from Old High German hônida, ‘dishonour’, and Middle Dutch hoonde.

history: Honte has a silent h that still matters. It comes from Frankish, and it begins with an h aspiré: you say la honte, never l'honte. The Frankish word, reconstructed as *hauniþa, meant scorn or mockery; the TLFi rebuilds it from Old High German hônida, ‘dishonour’, and Middle Dutch hoonde. In the Song of Roland, around 1100, hunte is dishonour. The related verb honnir, ‘to shame publicly’, is rare today, but many English speakers know it from the motto of the Order of the Garter: Honi soit qui mal y pense, ‘shame on whoever thinks ill of it’. In everyday French, avoir honte is ‘to be ashamed’, and c'est la honte ! is what young people say about something embarrassing.
historyEinfach: Honte comes from Frankish, the language of the Franks. It first meant ‘dishonour’. The h is not spoken, but it stops the article from changing: la honte, not l'honte. J'ai honte means ‘I am ashamed’.
